paragraphs: On fruits of a tree one recites the berachah "Borei Peri HaEtz" (Who creates the fruit of the tree), and on fruits of the ground one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah" (Who creates the fruit of the ground). The reason the Sages did not institute reciting "Borei Peri HaAretz" (Who creates the fruit of the land) is that the term "eretz" (land) is more praiseworthy than the term "adamah" (ground): first, the meaning expounded is that "eretz" is a term of favor (ratzon); and further, the term "eretz" is mentioned first in the Torah, in the verse of Bereishit, and it is also mentioned more in the account of the creation of the world, and moreover the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, is mentioned alongside it, as it is written (Bereishit 1:1), "In the beginning God created the heavens and the eretz," and it is written (ibid. 2:4), "on the day that the Lord God made eretz and heaven." Therefore, in order to accord honor to bread, which is more praiseworthy than the fruits of the ground, they reserved the term "eretz" for it alone, in the berachah "HaMotzi lechem min ha-aretz," while they placed the term "adamah" in the berachah on fruits. The Rav Shiyurei Berachah wrote that they instituted the term "adamah" in the berachah on fruits because there are fifty-five species of fruits of the ground, corresponding to the numerical value of the word "ha-adamah" - see there. It appears to me that this refers to the fruits that existed in the Land of Israel in their days, but in the world at large there are probably more than fifty-five species.

clarification.explanation: On fruits of a tree one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz," and on fruits of the ground one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah" - not "Borei Peri HaAretz," even though the term "eretz" (land) is more praiseworthy than the term "adamah" (ground) (it is a term of favor, and it is mentioned before "adamah" in the Torah, and even God's Name is mentioned alongside it in the verses of creation). The reason: in order to give special honor to bread, which is more praiseworthy than the fruits of the ground, they reserved the term "eretz" for it (in the berachah "HaMotzi lechem min ha-aretz"), and left the term "adamah" for the berachah on the other fruits. An additional reason: there are fifty-five species of fruits of the ground, corresponding to the numerical value of the word "ha-adamah" - though Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that this is true only regarding the fruits of the Land of Israel in their time, while in the wider world there are apparently more than fifty-five species.
takeaways: Fruits of a tree - the berachah "Borei Peri HaEtz"; fruits of the ground - "Borei Peri HaAdamah" (not "HaAretz," which is reserved for bread).
The reason: honor for the praiseworthy bread, and a numerical hint (55 species of ground-fruits, corresponding to the value of "ha-adamah").

paragraphs: Small, unripe tree fruits that are still sour - even though Maran ruled that if they are eaten only under duress (out of necessity) one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz," nevertheless the Acharonim wrote to recite "Shehakol," and only if they were cooked or corrected by fire does one recite "Borei Peri HaEtz," because while they were still raw they were eaten under duress. Therefore, small sour fruits that are cooked in a dish according to the custom of our town - if it is clear that they were eaten under duress while raw, one recites over them after cooking "Borei Peri HaEtz"; and if there is doubt whether they were eaten under duress before cooking, then one recites over them after cooking "Shehakol." This is because any fruit that is not eaten raw due to sourness, even under duress, if one eats it raw one does not recite any berachah over it at all, and if one eats it cooked one recites "Shehakol." Therefore, the fruit called in Arabic "narinj" (sour citrus fruit) which is picked while still small, when they are bitter as wormwood, and cooked in sugar - one does not recite over them after frying in sugar anything but "Shehakol"; see Mishb'tzot Zahav. To what does this apply? To a fruit that was picked before its ripening was complete and before it had grown to its full measure. But a fully-grown fruit whose nature is bitter, even though it remains on the tree many days, if one sweetens it by cooking with fire or by some other means, one recites over it its own berachah, whether it is a tree-fruit or a ground-fruit berachah. Therefore, olives, whose nature is bitter even after they have grown to their full measure, are blessed after their correction by pickling with their own berachah, which is "Borei Peri HaEtz," and so too anything similar to this.

clarification.explanation: Small tree fruits that have not yet ripened and are sour - even though Maran ruled that if they are eaten out of necessity one recites over them "Borei Peri HaEtz," the Acharonim wrote to recite over them "Shehakol," and only if they were cooked or corrected by fire does one recite "Borei Peri HaEtz" (because while still raw they were eaten only out of necessity). Therefore small sour fruits cooked in a dish according to local custom - if it is clear that they were eaten raw out of necessity, one recites over them after cooking "Borei Peri HaEtz"; and if there is doubt about this, one recites over them afterward only "Shehakol," for the rule is that a fruit not eaten raw due to excessive sourness (even under duress) receives no berachah at all while raw, and only after cooking does one recite "Shehakol" over it. Therefore sour citrus fruit picked small and cooked in sugar - one recites over it after frying only "Shehakol." However, a fully ripened fruit that is bitter by nature (like olives) - even if it would remain on the tree many days and not sweeten on its own - if it is corrected by cooking or pickling, one recites over it its regular berachah (tree or ground).
takeaways: A small, sour tree fruit eaten only under duress while raw, and later cooked: if it was eaten under duress while raw - the berachah "Borei Peri HaEtz"; if in doubt - "Shehakol."
A fruit that is bitter by nature (like olives) and is corrected by cooking/pickling receives its regular berachah, even though it never ripens naturally.

paragraphs: A fully-grown fruit that is fried or cooked - if its form is still recognizable, one recites its principal berachah; but if it has completely dissolved so that its form has changed, one recites "Shehakol." Therefore, those [fruits] that are soaked in water and mashed, called in Arabic "mishmish" (apricot), one recites "Shehakol," because the fruit has dissolved and its form has changed so that the fruit is no longer recognizable. Likewise, those who cook this fruit in a dish together with meat and the like, so that the form of the fruit dissolves - if one comes to eat it by itself, one recites "Shehakol." Likewise, the fruit-leather made from this fruit, called in Arabic "qamar al-din" (dried apricot sheet), one recites over it "Shehakol." Likewise, dates that are fried in a pan until they are made into a paste, called in Arabic "tamgiyya" (date preserve), one recites over it "Shehakol," because their form has changed. But dates that have been mashed somewhat by hand, so that their form has not changed and it is recognizable that they are dates, their berachah does not change.

clarification.explanation: A fully-grown fruit that is fried or cooked, as long as its original form is recognizable upon it, receives its principal berachah; but if it has dissolved completely and its form has changed entirely, one recites "Shehakol" over it. Therefore apricots that are soaked in water until they completely dissolve are blessed with "Shehakol," since they are no longer recognizable as fruit. The same applies to fruit cooked in a dish with meat until it dissolves, and one then eats it by itself - one recites "Shehakol"; likewise dried apricot leather and fried date preserve made into a paste - one recites "Shehakol" over them, since their form has changed. By contrast, dates that have been mashed somewhat by hand but are still recognizable as dates - their berachah does not change.
takeaways: A cooked or fried fruit that has completely changed form (mashed and no longer recognizable as fruit) - its berachah is "Shehakol."
A fruit only slightly mashed but still recognizable as fruit - its berachah remains as usual (tree/ground).

paragraphs: The peel of etrogim, or the peel of the fruit called in Arabic "burtuqal" (orange), which you are accustomed to cook in sugar - some say one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz," some say "Borei Peri HaAdamah," and some say "Shehakol"; and by the strict law one should recite "Shehakol" due to the doubt.

clarification.explanation: On the peel of etrogim or the peel of oranges cooked in sugar - there is a dispute among the halachic authorities: some say "Borei Peri HaEtz," some say "Borei Peri HaAdamah," and some say "Shehakol"; by the strict law one should recite "Shehakol" because of the doubt.
takeaways: Citrus peel cooked in sugar: one recites "Shehakol" because of the doubt among the various opinions.

paragraphs: Fruits that were soaked in water - even if there is a taste of the fruit in the water, if one drinks the water by itself, one recites "Shehakol." Therefore, the fruit called in Arabic "nabkhara" (dried Persian apricot), which is customarily soaked in water - if one comes to drink the water by itself, one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Fruits that are soaked in water - even if there is a taste of the fruit in the water, if one drinks the water by itself (and not the fruit itself), one recites "Shehakol." Therefore, dried Persian apricot ("nabkhara"), which is customarily soaked in water, if one wishes to drink only the water by itself, one recites "Shehakol."
takeaways: Drinking water in which fruit has been soaked (without eating the fruit itself) - its berachah is "Shehakol," even if the water has a fruit taste.

paragraphs: Tree fruits that are good both when raw and when cooked - one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" whether one eats them raw or cooked. And if it is not customary to eat them raw but only cooked, then if one eats them raw one recites "Shehakol," and if cooked one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz." The same law applies to ground-fruits and vegetables as well. Likewise, if they are cooked and better than when raw, if one eats them raw one recites "Shehakol," and if cooked one recites their principal berachah.

clarification.explanation: Tree fruits that are good both raw and cooked - one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" in either case, whether eaten raw or cooked. But if it is customary to eat them only cooked and not raw - if one eats them raw nonetheless, one recites "Shehakol"; and if cooked, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz." The same law applies to ground-fruits and vegetables as well. Likewise, if they are better cooked than raw (but can also be eaten raw), and one eats them raw, one recites "Shehakol," and cooked - their principal berachah.
takeaways: A fruit/vegetable customarily eaten only cooked: raw - the berachah "Shehakol"; cooked - its regular berachah (tree/ground).

paragraphs: Ground-fruits and vegetables that are better raw than if cooked in water alone - even though one now cooks them together with something else, in sugar or meat and the like, and they are improved by this cooking more than they would be if eaten raw, nevertheless one does not recite over them, while cooked, anything but "Shehakol," and does not recite their own berachah, because if they had been cooked in water alone without the admixture of something else they would be considered inferior [to raw], and therefore the significance of the other thing cooked with them does not help them, even though they are improved by it - so is the opinion of the Turei Zahav and those who agree with him. And although there are those who disagree, we hold that in a case of doubt regarding berachot we are lenient, and therefore one recites "Shehakol." And all this applies specifically to vegetables or ground-fruits; but tree fruits - even though if they were cooked alone in water they would be inferior to eating them raw, requiring "Shehakol" - nevertheless, if they are cooked with something else and are thereby improved, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" according to all opinions. Therefore, cucumbers, called in Arabic "khiyar," which is a ground-fruit, and which are cooked with meat - even though this cooking improves them - if one wishes to eat it by itself now, after it was cooked with the meat and improved, one does not recite over it "Borei Peri HaAdamah" but rather "Shehakol," because this fruit called "khiyar," if it had been cooked alone in water, would be inferior, requiring "Shehakol" over it, and therefore even now, when it was cooked with meat, one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Ground-fruits and vegetables that are better raw than if cooked in water alone - even though they are now cooked together with something else (sugar, meat) and are thereby improved even beyond how they would be raw - one still recites over them, while cooked, only "Shehakol" and not their regular berachah, since had they been cooked in water alone without any addition they would be considered inferior, and the addition of the other significant ingredient cooked with them does not change this, even though it improves them (so holds the Turei Zahav and those who concur with him). And although there are those who disagree, the halachah follows the rule that in a case of doubt regarding berachot we are lenient, and therefore one recites "Shehakol." This applies specifically to vegetables and ground-fruits; but tree fruits - even if they would be inferior when cooked in water alone compared to raw - if they are cooked with something else and thereby improved, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" over them according to all opinions. Therefore a cucumber (a ground-fruit) cooked with meat - even though it is improved by this cooking - if one eats it by itself, one recites "Shehakol."
takeaways: A ground-fruit or vegetable that would be inferior if cooked in water alone: even if it is improved by cooking together with something else (meat, sugar) - its berachah remains "Shehakol."
A tree fruit, by contrast: if it is improved by cooking with something else, one recites its regular berachah (tree) according to all opinions.

paragraphs: All fruits that are planted to be eaten cooked, and it is not their way to be eaten raw at all - if one eats them raw, one recites "Shehakol"; if one eats them cooked, one recites their principal berachah. Therefore the fruit called in Arabic "lubya" (a type of bean, cowpea) and the fruit called "badinjan" (eggplant), which are ground-fruits - if one eats them raw, one recites "Shehakol"; if one eats them cooked, one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah," if one eats them by themselves. There are two reasons for this: one, that they were planted with the intention of being eaten cooked, and it is not their way to be eaten raw as they are cooked; and there is a further reason here, that these are better eaten cooked than eaten raw, and we wrote above that in such a case, eating them raw, one recites "Shehakol." Therefore on the night of Rosh HaShanah, when this fruit called "lubya" is eaten as a good omen, if one eats it raw, one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Fruits planted specifically to be eaten cooked, and it is not their way to be eaten raw at all - if one eats them raw, one recites "Shehakol"; if one eats them cooked, one recites their principal berachah. Therefore beans ("lubya") and eggplant, which are ground-fruits - if eaten raw: "Shehakol"; cooked: "Borei Peri HaAdamah." There are two reasons for this: they were planted for cooked consumption, and they are also better eaten cooked. Therefore, on the night of Rosh HaShanah, when "lubya" is eaten as a good omen, if eaten raw, one recites "Shehakol."
takeaways: A fruit/vegetable meant from the outset to be eaten only cooked (such as beans, eggplant): raw - "Shehakol"; cooked - its regular berachah.
Example: "lubya" on the night of Rosh HaShanah - if eaten raw, its berachah is "Shehakol."

paragraphs: Honey that flows from dates, whether on its own or by squeezing, one recites "Shehakol." The same law applies to the liquids that come out of all types of fruits, whether they came out on their own or by squeezing - one recites "Shehakol." But the liquid that comes out of grapes, whether on its own or by squeezing, one recites "Borei Peri HaGafen." Likewise, the liquid that comes out of olives is considered like the body of the fruit itself, and one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz," like the berachah of the fruit. Black watermelons, called in Arabic "raqqi," sometimes have water collected inside them - if one drinks the water by itself and does not eat from the fruit of the watermelons, one recites "Shehakol"; but if one also eats from the fruit itself, one need not recite a berachah [on the water], since the berachah on the fruit exempts it. The same law applies to nuts that come from the lands of India, called "jawz al-hind" (coconut) - inside the nut there is found water like milk; if one drinks it by itself, one recites "Shehakol," and if one eats from the fruit, one need not recite a berachah over that water.

clarification.explanation: Honey that flows from dates (whether on its own or by squeezing) is blessed with "Shehakol," and so too all liquids that come out of every type of fruit (on their own or by squeezing) - "Shehakol." However, the liquid that comes out of grapes is blessed with "Borei Peri HaGafen," and the liquid that comes out of olives is considered the body of the fruit itself, and one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" over it, as the berachah of the fruit. In a black watermelon that sometimes has water collected inside it - if one drinks only the water (without eating from the fruit itself), one recites "Shehakol"; but if one also eats from the fruit itself, the berachah on the fruit exempts the water as well. The same applies to a coconut, which contains a milk-like liquid inside it - if one drinks it alone, "Shehakol"; and if one also eats from the fruit, there is no need for a separate berachah on the liquid.
takeaways: Juice/liquid that comes out of most fruits - "Shehakol"; exceptions: grape juice - "Borei Peri HaGafen," olive liquid - "Borei Peri HaEtz" (as the fruit itself).
A natural liquid inside a fruit (watermelon water, coconut water): if drunk alone - "Shehakol"; if one also eats from the fruit - the berachah on the fruit exempts it.

paragraphs: Coffee that has been boiled and made into a beverage - even though there is a dispute regarding its berachah, the custom has already spread everywhere to recite "Shehakol." And if one eats it roasted, whether the beans remain whole or it has been ground into flour-like powder - even though the Acharonim agreed to recite "Borei Peri HaAdamah," I have ruled in my holy work Mekabtziel to recite "Shehakol." Likewise on the beverage called "chay" (tea) one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Coffee that has been boiled and made into a beverage - although there is a dispute regarding its berachah, the custom has already spread everywhere to recite "Shehakol" over it. And roasted coffee, whether still in beans or ground into flour - although the Acharonim agreed to recite "Borei Peri HaAdamah," Rabbi Yosef Chaim rules in his work "Mekabtziel" to recite "Shehakol." Likewise, on tea one recites "Shehakol."
takeaways: Coffee (as a beverage, or roasted/ground) and tea - their berachah in practice is "Shehakol," despite other opinions requiring "Borei Peri HaAdamah."

paragraphs: Chickpeas, called in Arabic "hummus," when roasted - one recites over them "Borei Peri HaAdamah," and after them "Borei Nefashot Rabot." And if one grinds them until they become like flour, one recites "Shehakol," and all the more so if sugar is mixed with them, in which case one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Roasted chickpeas ("hummus") - one recites over them "Borei Peri HaAdamah," and afterward "Borei Nefashot Rabot." If ground until they become like flour - one recites "Shehakol," and all the more so if sugar is mixed in - likewise "Shehakol."
takeaways: Whole roasted chickpeas - "Borei Peri HaAdamah"; ground into flour (or mixed with sugar) - "Shehakol."

paragraphs: Here in our town they make a kind of sweet called "simsimiyya," in which sesame is mixed with sugar or with honey - one must recite "Borei Peri HaAdamah," because the sesame is the primary component. Likewise, sesame mixed with a sour ingredient, called "summaq" (sumac) and "za'atar" (hyssop), one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah," since the sesame is primary. But on the waste of pressed sesame, called in Arabic "kasba" (sesame press residue), one recites "Shehakol," because the form of the sesame has changed - see Chesed L'Avraham, chamber 3, chidush gimel. Likewise, on ground sesame, called in Arabic "gashi" (tahini), one recites "Shehakol." Also here in our town it is customary to mash dates with sesame, calling it in Arabic "madguga" (a spread of tahini and dates) - the strict law is that if they have been completely mashed so that the form of the dates is not recognizable, one recites "Shehakol," and if pieces of the dates still remain that are recognizable as dates, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" and it exempts the rest.

clarification.explanation: A local sweet ("simsimiyya") that mixes sesame with sugar or honey - one should recite "Borei Peri HaAdamah," because the sesame is the primary component; likewise sesame mixed with sharp herbs ("summaq" and "za'atar") - the sesame is primary. But on the residue of pressed sesame ("kasba") one recites "Shehakol," because the form of the sesame has completely changed; and likewise on ground sesame (tahini) - "Shehakol." A date-sesame spread ("madguga") - if it has been completely mashed so that the form of the dates is not recognizable, one recites "Shehakol"; and if recognizable pieces of dates remain, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz" and it exempts the rest.
takeaways: Sesame mixed with sugar/honey/sharp herbs (sesame is primary) - "Borei Peri HaAdamah."
Ground sesame (tahini) or the residue of its pressing - "Shehakol," since its form has changed.
A date-sesame spread: if pieces of dates are recognizable - "Borei Peri HaEtz"; if completely mashed - "Shehakol."

paragraphs: Roses that are prepared with sugar, called in Arabic "ma'gun al-ward" (rose beverage), one recites over them "Shehakol," for one reason, that the form of the rose is not recognizable, and further, even if it should happen that the form of the rose is recognizable in it, since it is not the custom here in our town for healthy people to eat this except as a medicine, one recites "Shehakol."

clarification.explanation: A sweet rose beverage in sugar - one recites over it "Shehakol," since the form of the rose is not recognizable, and even were it recognizable - since it is not customary here for healthy people to drink it except as a remedy - the berachah is "Shehakol."
takeaways: A rose beverage in sugar - "Shehakol," both because the form of the rose is not recognizable and because it is meant for medicinal use rather than ordinary consumption.

paragraphs: If one drinks strong liquor (shechar), and in order to sweeten its sharpness eats some fruit afterward, since his intention is not to eat that fruit but rather [to assist] the liquor, the liquor is primary and it exempts the fruit, which is secondary; therefore by the strict law one should not recite a berachah over the fruit. There are those who disagree and require a berachah; therefore one who fears Heaven should be careful to eat from the fruit before drinking the liquor, and recite the berachah then on the fruit [as primary]. This is the rule in the laws of berachot: whatever is primary, and mixed with it is something secondary, one recites the berachah on the primary and it exempts the secondary. Therefore, in all kinds of preserves, the sugar is exempted by the berachah on the fruit, because the fruits are primary and the sugar is secondary. And the kinds of sweets called in Arabic "rahat lokum" (Turkish delight), in which flour called "nasha" (starch) is mixed with sugar, and likewise what is called "zalabiya" (starch sweets in sugar), which some call "zangula" - since the starch is primary and the sugar is secondary, one recites over them "Borei Minei Mezonot." And so the custom has spread here in our town of Baghdad, to recite "Borei Minei Mezonot" over this and over that.

clarification.explanation: One who drinks strong liquor (shechar) and eats fruit afterward to sweeten its sharpness - since his intention is not to eat the fruit itself but only to help with the liquor, the liquor is primary and exempts the fruit, which is secondary; therefore by the strict law one should not recite a separate berachah on the fruit. There are those who disagree and require a berachah on the fruit regardless; therefore one who fears Heaven should be careful to eat the fruit before drinking the liquor and recite the berachah then, while it is primary. The rule in the laws of berachot: whenever there is a primary item with a secondary item mixed in, one recites the berachah on the primary item and it exempts the secondary - and so too in all kinds of preserves, where the fruit is primary and the sugar is secondary and is exempted by its berachah. In a certain sweet (Turkish delight, zalabiya) where the starch/flour is primary and the sugar is secondary, one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot."
takeaways: With a primary item and a secondary item (such as fruit eaten to sweeten liquor) - the berachah on the primary exempts the secondary; it is proper to eat the fruit first and recite its own berachah separately.
In a sweet where the starch/flour is primary and the sugar secondary - the berachah is "Borei Minei Mezonot."

paragraphs: Whole almonds coated in sugar - it was the practice of the crown of my head, my father, of blessed memory, when he ate them, to separate the sugar from them and recite over the almonds "Borei Peri HaEtz" and over the sugar "Shehakol." But the custom of the people of our town is to recite over them "Shehakol" and to eat them as they are without separating them from each other. See Eliyah Rabbah, siman 204, se'if 17, and Eshel Avraham, se'if katan 25, who wrote that even if there is much sugar, one recites "HaEtz" - see there. And afterward the book Yosef Ometz of the Ashkenazi came to our town, and it is written on page 51 in accordance with the custom of the crown of my head, my master, my father, of blessed memory; and so it is fitting to rule.

clarification.explanation: Whole almonds coated in sugar - Rabbi Yosef Chaim's father used to separate the sugar from the almonds and recite over the almonds "Borei Peri HaEtz" and over the sugar "Shehakol," separately. But the custom of the town (Baghdad) was to recite "Shehakol" over them and eat them as they are without separating; afterward the book "Yosef Ometz" arrived in the town, and it was written there in accordance with his father's custom - and so Rabbi Yosef Chaim ruled, "and so it is fitting to instruct," meaning to separate the sugar from the almonds and recite two berachot.
takeaways: Almonds coated in sugar: the ruling in practice is to separate the sugar from the almonds and recite "Borei Peri HaEtz" over the almonds and "Shehakol" over the sugar (even though the town custom was to recite "Shehakol" over them together).

paragraphs: On sugar that comes from cane - even though some say to recite "Borei Peri HaEtz," the custom has spread to recite "Shehakol," because of the doubt regarding berachot, to be lenient. And if one has before him a tree-fruit and sugar, Eliyah Rabbah, siman 202, se'if katan 4, wrote to recite first over the sugar "Shehakol" and afterward recite over the fruit, and not to do the reverse. However, Rav Peri Megadim, in the introduction to the laws of berachot, page 12 side a, wrote: if one has before him a tree-fruit, and also another fruit about which there is doubt whether its berachah is "Borei Peri HaEtz" or "Borei Peri HaAdamah," one should recite first over the certain one, intending to exempt only the certain one and not the doubtful one, and afterward recite "Borei Peri HaAdamah" over the doubtful one - see there. And in my responsa Rav Pe'alim I ruled like Eliyah Rabbah, to recite first over the doubtful one. However, if one forgot and recited first over the certain one, one should recite afterward over the sugar as well, since certainly when he recited over the certain one he did not intend to exempt the sugar; and it is specifically as the preferable practice, ab initio, that we act to give precedence to the sugar. And if one has before him a fruit whose berachah is certainly "HaEtz," and a fruit whose berachah is certainly "HaAdamah," and a fruit about which there is doubt, whose law is to recite "Shehakol" - if we say that in this case one should give precedence to reciting "Shehakol" over the doubtful one and afterward recite over the certain ones, in order to gain a berachah, or perhaps this would be considered "causing an unnecessary berachah," since one could have recited first over the certain "HaEtz" and "HaAdamah" and intended thereby to exempt the doubtful one as well - I explained there in the holy work Rav Pe'alim that one should do this, giving precedence to the doubtful one, and that there is no concern here of an unnecessary berachah, and I found my reasoning stated explicitly in the book Chemed Moshe, and I brought proofs for this. But afterward I brought the words of our teacher the Gaon Rabbenu Zalman in his Shulchan Aruch, siman 249, se'if 11, who holds that in such a case there is a prohibition of an unnecessary berachah. And in the end I ruled, with the help of Heaven, that on a weekday one should give precedence to the certain and intend to exempt the doubtful one; but on Shabbat, when one should increase in berachot, one may give precedence to the doubtful one first and gain an additional berachah - and see Erech HaShulchan, siman 211, se'if katan 3, who concludes that on Shabbat and Yom Tov this is permitted in such a case - see there.

clarification.explanation: On cane sugar - even though some say to recite "Borei Peri HaEtz," the custom has spread to recite "Shehakol," out of doubt regarding berachot, to be lenient. If one has before him a tree-fruit and sugar - some hold that one should first recite over the sugar ("Shehakol") and then over the fruit; and some hold that one should first recite over the certain item (the fruit) and intend to exempt only it, and afterward recite over the doubtful item (the sugar). Rabbi Yosef Chaim rules that one should give precedence to the doubtful item, but if one forgot and recited over the certain item first, one should recite over the sugar separately as well. In a case where one has before him a certain tree-fruit, a certain ground-fruit, and also a doubtful fruit (whose law is "Shehakol") - a further question arises: is it proper to give precedence to the doubtful item, in order to "gain" a berachah, or is this perhaps a prohibited "unnecessary berachah," since one could give precedence to the certain items and intend thereby to exempt the doubtful one too and save a berachah? Rabbi Yosef Chaim himself first wrote in his work "Rav Pe'alim" that it is permitted, and even proper, to give precedence to the doubtful item, and that there is no concern of an unnecessary berachah here, finding support for this in the book "Chemed Moshe"; but afterward he found that Rabbenu Zalman (the Baal HaTanya), in his Shulchan Aruch (siman 249), holds that there is a prohibition of an unnecessary berachah in this. Therefore Rabbi Yosef Chaim concluded, in practice: on a weekday one should give precedence to the certain item and intend to exempt the doubtful one (so as not to enter the concern of the prohibition); but on Shabbat, when there is a value in increasing berachot, one may give precedence to the doubtful item in order to "gain" an additional berachah, and he brought that the "Erech HaShulchan" also agrees that on Shabbat and Yom Tov this is permitted.
takeaways: Cane sugar - its berachah is "Shehakol," out of doubt.
A tree-fruit and sugar together: one always gives precedence to the sugar (the doubtful item) and then the fruit - even on a weekday.

There is a dispute whether giving precedence to the doubtful item in order to gain a berachah is considered a prohibited "unnecessary berachah" - Rabbenu Zalman (the Baal HaTanya) held that it is prohibited, while Rabbi Yosef Chaim himself initially leaned to permit it; the halachah was ultimately set to distinguish between a weekday and Shabbat.

If one has a certain tree-fruit, a certain ground-fruit, and a doubtful item before him: on a weekday, give precedence to the certain items (and intend thereby to exempt the doubtful one); on Shabbat, one may give precedence to the doubtful item to gain an additional berachah.

paragraphs: Anything mixed with one of the five species of grain in order to give flavor to the mixture, one recites over it "Mezonot"; but if it is only for binding, it is secondary and nullified within the dish. To what does this apply? To the five species of grain; but other kinds of food mixed with each other - if each one is recognizable by itself, one recites over each one the berachah appropriate to it; and if they have been mashed and stuck together, one follows the majority, and recites the berachah of the majority, which exempts the other. And when one puts flour into an almond dish prepared for a sick person - if this is done so that it will nourish the heart, one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot"; but if only to bind it, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz." And since there is room for doubt whether they also intend that it should nourish the heart, it is therefore proper to be stringent and eat it within a full meal, or to also eat "pat kisanin" and tree-fruit; and anyone in a similar case, one who fears Heaven should satisfy all the opinions, as mentioned in Chesed L'Alafim, siman 207, ot 4 - see there.

clarification.explanation: Anything mixed with one of the five species of grain (wheat, barley, etc.) for the sake of flavor in the mixture - one recites "Mezonot" over it; but if the grain serves only to bind (as with binding flour), it is secondary and nullified within the dish, and does not affect the berachah. This applies only to the five species of grain; but other types of food mixed with each other - if each one is recognizable by itself, one recites over each its own berachah; and if they have been mashed and stuck together, one follows the majority, reciting the berachah of the majority, which exempts the minority. When flour is put into an almond dish made for a sick person - if the intention is to nourish the heart (for nutrition), one recites "Mezonot"; if only to bind, one recites "Borei Peri HaEtz"; and since there is doubt about the intention, it is proper to be stringent and eat this within a regular meal, or to also eat "pat kisanin" and tree-fruit, so as to fulfill one's obligation under all possibilities.
takeaways: Grain mixed in for the sake of flavor - the berachah is "Mezonot"; grain used only for binding - it is secondary and nullified, and does not determine the berachah.
Non-grain ingredients mixed together: if each is recognizable - a separate berachah for each; if mashed together - one follows the majority.

paragraphs: Cooked rice, whether the dish called in Arabic "pilaw" (whole rice grains) or the dish called "shorba" (rice dissolved in soup) in which the rice has been mashed, one recites first "Borei Minei Mezonot" and afterward "Borei Nefashot Rabot." And even though there are those who say that if it has not been completely mashed to the point that the grains stick to each other, one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah," the custom has already spread to recite "Borei Minei Mezonot" in every case. And if one ate this rice and also ate "pat kisanin," even though he ate one separately and the other separately, one recites "Me'ein Shalosh" over the "kisanin," and it exempts the rice as well in this berachah - and not like the Rav HaMagiah in Chesed L'Alafim, siman 208, ot 19, who wrote to recite "Borei Nefashot Rabot" first on the rice and afterward "Me'ein Shalosh" on the "kisanin," for there is reason to question this, on account of an unnecessary berachah.

clarification.explanation: Cooked rice - whether "pilaw" (whole rice grains) or "shorba" (rice dissolved in soup) - one recites first "Borei Minei Mezonot" and finally "Borei Nefashot Rabot." And although some say that if it has not been completely mashed to the point that the grains stick together one recites "Borei Peri HaAdamah" - the custom has already spread to recite "Borei Minei Mezonot" in every case. And if one ate this rice and also "pat haba'ah b'kisanin" (pastry), even though he ate each one separately - one recites "Me'ein Shalosh" over the pastry, and it exempts the rice as well; and not like the opinion of the glossator on "Chesed L'Alafim" who wrote to recite first "Borei Nefashot" over the rice and afterward "Me'ein Shalosh" over the pastry, for there is reason to question this on account of an unnecessary berachah.
takeaways: Cooked rice (pilaw or shorba) - "Borei Minei Mezonot" and finally "Borei Nefashot," in every case.
One who ate rice and also "pat kisanin" - "Me'ein Shalosh" over the pastry exempts the rice too (so as not to multiply berachot).

paragraphs: One who eats "pat kisanin" up to fifty-four dirhams, which is a measure of three eggs, recites "Me'ein Shalosh," because such an amount is not considered a fixed meal (keviut se'udah). And on seventy-two dirhams one recites Birkat HaMazon according to all opinions, since this is considered a fixed meal according to all opinions. But from fifty-four dirhams to seventy-two dirhams, some say one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh," and some say one recites "HaMotzi" and Birkat HaMazon; and although the strict law requires that one not recite Birkat HaMazon in this case, on account of doubt regarding berachot, and whoever does not recite Birkat HaMazon should consequently also not recite "HaMotzi" but only "Borei Minei Mezonot," so that his berachot do not contradict each other, as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbenu Zalman, siman 168, se'if 12 - nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should be careful not to bring himself into this measure at all, but should either eat less than fifty-four dirhams and recite "Me'ein Shalosh," or eat more than seventy-two dirhams and recite Birkat HaMazon according to all opinions - see the Acharonim. And if from the outset one intended to eat a little less than fifty-four dirhams and recited "Borei Minei Mezonot," and afterward continued eating and ate a measure of a fixed meal according to all opinions, which is more than seventy-two dirhams, he must recite Birkat HaMazon even though he first recited "Mezonot," and his berachot turn out to contradict each other, because only ab initio must one be careful about this, that his berachot not contradict each other.

clarification.explanation: One who eats "pat kisanin" up to a measure of fifty-four dirhams (about the size of three eggs) recites "Me'ein Shalosh," since this is not considered a fixed meal. Above seventy-two dirhams, one recites Birkat HaMazon according to all opinions, since this is considered a full fixed meal. Between fifty-four and seventy-two dirhams there is a dispute: some say "Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh," and some say "HaMotzi" and Birkat HaMazon. The rule in practice: due to doubt regarding berachot, one should not recite Birkat HaMazon in this middle range, and so that the berachot not contradict each other, one also does not recite "HaMotzi" but only "Mezonot." Nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should be careful to avoid this middle measure altogether - eating less than fifty-four dirhams (and reciting "Me'ein Shalosh"), or more than seventy-two (and reciting Birkat HaMazon). If one had intended from the outset to eat a small amount and already recited "Mezonot," but then continued and ate a full fixed-meal measure (above seventy-two), he must recite Birkat HaMazon nonetheless, even though he first recited "Mezonot" - since one need only be careful about contradicting berachot ab initio.
takeaways: "Pat kisanin": less than fifty-four dirhams - "Me'ein Shalosh"; above seventy-two dirhams - Birkat HaMazon according to all opinions; in between - a dispute, and in practice one recites "Mezonot" first and "Me'ein Shalosh" at the end.
It is preferable to avoid eating the disputed measure; if one mistakenly ate more than seventy-two after already reciting "Mezonot," one recites Birkat HaMazon nonetheless.

paragraphs: What is called "pat kisanin" according to all opinions? A dough kneaded with honey, or with butter, or with milk, or with oil, or with fruit juice and wine, or with other beverages, where the majority is honey or butter and the like and the minority is flour - this is "pat kisanin" according to all opinions, over which one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh." And the same law applies to bread made in the shape of pockets, called in Arabic "sambusak" (dough pockets filled), which are filled before baking with sugar and almonds or nuts or other kinds of fruit and spices - even though the dough itself was kneaded with water alone, and even though they are baked in an oven without any beverage at all - nevertheless they are considered "pat kisanin" according to all opinions, over which one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh." But dough kneaded with water alone, made before baking into pockets and filled with meat or fish or cheese, is not "pat kisanin" according to all opinions, because some say that since meat, cheese, and fish come in any case to accompany bread, they do not nullify the dough from the category of bread - which differs from those pockets filled with nuts and sugar and other fruits, which are not normally used to accompany bread. And there are those who disagree and hold that since they do not resemble complete bread, they have the law of "kisanin" and one recites over them "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh." Likewise, dough kneaded with water alone, not spiced and not filled, but made into dry cakes that are gnawed for appetite - here too there is the aforementioned dispute, and for practical halachah we hold, in both this case and that case, to recite "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh," since one should not recite Birkat HaMazon in a case of doubt, because it multiplies berachot; and as for the berachah "HaMotzi," even though it does not multiply, nevertheless, since one recites the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh," one must recite "Mezonot," for if one recites "HaMotzi" his berachot will contradict one another. And Chesed L'Alafim, siman 168, ot 8, wrote: if one mixed into the dough honey or oil or spices and the taste of the mixture is not recognizable in the dough, this is complete bread, and the fact that they make it into shapes of rolls different from the shape of bread makes no difference. And a man who fears God, if he wishes to recite "Borei Minei Mezonot," should at least put in oil or seasonings in a quantity that will be recognizable and perceptible, or make it into dry cakes that are gnawed, called "biscuit," since there is an opinion that these are considered "pat haba'ah b'kisanin" - so far his words. And here in our town, may it be built and established, it is customary to make thin small rolls, called in Arabic "gradak" (thin, crisp wafers) or "ba'abe'a" (bread wafers with much oil and spices), and they are made from dough of thick consistency in which sesame oil is placed, and some also place a spice called in Arabic "hawayij" (caraway), and one recites over them "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh"; and one must caution them to put in oil in a sufficient measure that it be recognizable and perceptible to the palate when tasted for eating, and certainly those who also put in the aforementioned spice, it is preferable, since the spice is more perceptible and recognizable - but not everyone is willing to add the aforementioned spice.

clarification.explanation:
"Pat haba'ah b'kisanin" according to all opinions: dough kneaded with honey, butter, milk, oil, fruit juice, wine, or other beverages, where the majority is honey/butter and the like and the minority is flour - this is "pat kisanin" according to all opinions, over which one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" and the berachah "Me'ein Shalosh." The same law applies to pocket-shaped bread ("sambusak") filled before baking with sugar, almonds, nuts, or other fruits and spices - even though the dough itself was kneaded with water alone and baked in an oven without any beverage - it is considered "pat kisanin" according to all opinions.
But dough kneaded with water alone, made into pockets and filled with meat, fish, or cheese, is not "pat kisanin" according to all opinions: some say that since meat/cheese/fish in any case accompany bread, they do not nullify the dough from the category of bread (unlike nut-and-sugar fillings, which do not normally accompany bread); and there are those who disagree, holding that since they do not resemble complete bread, they have the law of "kisanin." Likewise, dough kneaded with water alone, unspiced and unfilled, made into dry cakes gnawed for appetite - here too there is the same dispute. In practice, in both cases, one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh" - since one should not recite Birkat HaMazon in a case of doubt (which multiplies berachot), and consequently, since one recites "Me'ein Shalosh," one must recite "Mezonot" (for "HaMotzi" would make the berachot contradict each other).
And "Chesed L'Alafim" wrote: if one mixed honey, oil, or spices into the dough and the taste of the mixture is not recognizable, this is complete bread, and its unusual shape makes no difference; and one who fears God, if he wishes to recite "Mezonot," should put in oil or seasoning in a measure that is recognizable and perceptible, or make dry cakes ("biscuits"). In our town it is customary to make thin small rolls made from a thick dough with sesame oil (some add caraway spice), and one recites over them "Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh" - one must caution that the oil be added in a measure recognizable to the palate; and those who also add the spice, it is preferable, though not everyone wishes to add it.
takeaways: "Pat kisanin" according to all opinions: dough that is mostly honey/oil/beverage, or filled with sugar/nuts/fruit (like sambusak) - "Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh."
Filled with meat/fish/cheese, or dry cakes made from water-dough - a dispute, and in practice one recites "Mezonot" and "Me'ein Shalosh."
One who wishes to recite "Mezonot" should add oil/spices in a measure recognizable to the palate.

paragraphs: Complete bread that has been crumbled into small pieces, none of which contains even a quarter of an olive's volume, but the form of bread is still recognizable in them - this is what is called in Arabic "meges" (bread crumbs in sugar and spices) - which are mixed with date honey and the like and eaten: one must first bring a piece of bread the size of an olive, wash one's hands, and recite "HaMotzi" over it, and afterward eat this "meges," and recite Birkat HaMazon.

clarification.explanation: Complete bread that has been crumbled into small pieces (less than a quarter of an olive's volume each), but the form of bread is still recognizable, mixed with date honey and the like (a dish called "meges") - one must first bring a whole piece of bread the size of an olive, wash one's hands, and recite "HaMotzi" over it, and only afterward eat the "meges," concluding with Birkat HaMazon.
takeaways: A dish of recognizable bread crumbs mixed with a sweetener ("meges") requires first washing the hands and reciting "HaMotzi" over a whole piece of bread the size of an olive, and only then eating the mixture.

paragraphs: If one eats "pat kisanin" during a meal in which he has already eaten complete bread, he does not recite a berachah over the "kisanin," because the berachah on the bread that he recited, "HaMotzi," exempts it. But if he brought some kind of sweet "kisanin" for dessert at the end of the meal, some say one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" over it, and some say one does not recite a berachah. Therefore, those who are accustomed to bring during the meal "zalabiya" (sweetened, fried starch dough) or "rahat lokum" (sweetened starch and sugar), which are made from flour called "nasha" (starch) and sugar - which we wrote above have the berachah "Borei Minei Mezonot" - should be careful to bring along with them something else whose berachah is "Shehakol," and recite "Shehakol" over it, intending to exempt these with this berachah of "Shehakol," and then eat from them during the meal, and upon him will come the berachah of goodness.

clarification.explanation: If one eats "pat haba'ah b'kisanin" during a meal in which he has already eaten complete bread, he does not recite a berachah on the "kisanin," since the berachah of "HaMotzi" exempts it. But if he brought some sweet "kisanin" for dessert at the end of the meal - some say one recites "Borei Minei Mezonot" over it, and some say one does not recite a berachah. Therefore, those accustomed to bring "zalabiya" or "rahat lokum" during the meal (made of starch and sugar, whose berachah is "Mezonot" as explained above) - should be careful to also bring something else whose berachah is "Shehakol," recite "Shehakol" over it, intend to exempt these sweets with this berachah as well, and only then eat from them during the meal - and this brings the blessing of good practice.
takeaways: "Pat kisanin" during a meal that includes bread - is exempted by "HaMotzi."
Sweet "kisanin" for dessert - a dispute whether a berachah is recited; therefore one should recite "Shehakol" over something else and intend to exempt them as well.
